tags.description:
A Mist account can be linked to OAuth2 providers:
1. First, login with your Mist account
2. Obtain the Authorization URL for Linking with [Get Oauth 2 Authorization Url for Login](/#operations/getOauth2AuthorizationUrlForLogin).
As OAuth2 flow goes through provider's UI and back with the authorization code, there are two ways to get it:
  * in JSON response, more usable for developers. Simply don\'t specify the `forward` parameter when obtaining the authorization URL
  * as GET parameter, for UI where the user flow can be continued. Specify the landing page/url of your choice 
3. Obtain the authorization code by clicking / going through Authorization URL Link Mist Account against OAuth2 Provider by using the authorization code
tags.name: Admins Login - OAuth2

tags.description:
API tokens with `oauth_enabled` set can be used as OAuth2 clients. This enables third-party applications (including MCP integrations) to obtain short-lived access tokens on behalf of a user, with explicit user consent.

The flow uses the standard OAuth2 authorization code grant (RFC 6749) with PKCE (RFC 7636) and rotating refresh tokens.

The OAuth endpoints are org-less: the `client_id` is a composite `<org_id>.<token_id>` (returned as `oauth_client_id` by the [Org API Token](/#operations/getOrgApiToken) endpoints), so a single credential encodes both the org and the client.

A third-party (server-side) web application must have its `redirect_uri` pre-registered on the token via `oauth_redirect_uris`; the value is matched exactly at authorize time. Native and CLI clients (e.g. MCP tools) use a loopback `redirect_uri` (`http://127.0.0.1[:port]`), which is always allowed with PKCE and does not need to be registered.

**Flow**
1. The application redirects the user's browser to [Get OAuth2 Authorization](/#operations/getOauthAuthorization)
2. After consent, the application receives an authorization code on its `redirect_uri` from [Grant OAuth2 Authorization](/#operations/grantOauthAuthorization)
3. The application exchanges the code, then later the refresh tokens, at [Exchange OAuth2 Token](/#operations/exchangeOauthToken)
4. The access token is used as `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`
tags.name: Orgs OAuth2

post.description:
Authenticate an administrator with email and password. A successful login creates the browser session cookies, including the `csrftoken` value used with the `X-CSRFToken` header on later API requests.

When 2FA is enabled, either include the `two_factor` code in this request or submit the first factor here and complete the login with [Two Factor](/#operations/twoFactor).
Check the login method for an administrator email address. This public lookup is mainly used by UI clients to determine whether the user should continue with local login or be redirected to SSO.

get.description:
Validate an OAuth2 authorization code request and return the consent page data. The third-party application redirects the user's browser here.

The `client_id` is the composite `<org_id>.<token_id>` returned as `oauth_client_id` by the [Org API Token](/#operations/getOrgApiToken) endpoints. The API token must have `oauth_enabled` set.

If the user is not authenticated, a `401` is returned with an `authorize_url` to resume the flow after login.

post.description:
The user has consented. Generate a single-use authorization code (valid for 60 seconds) and redirect the user to the client `redirect_uri` with `code` and `state` query parameters.

**Privilege coverage**

To prevent privilege escalation, the consenting user must hold **at least** the role the API token grants for every scope the token covers. Otherwise the request is rejected with a `400` and `{"detail": "access_denied: insufficient privileges to authorize this application"}`.

Coverage is hierarchy-aware, mirroring the runtime API permission model: a role at a higher scope covers the scopes beneath it (e.g. an org admin can authorize a site-scoped token, and an MSP admin can authorize an org-scoped token). A user with only a lower-scope privilege cannot authorize a token scoped above it.

Exchange an authorization code for an access token and a refresh token (`grant_type`==`authorization_code`), or rotate a refresh token for a new access token and a new refresh token (`grant_type`==`refresh_token`). Called server-to-server by the third-party application.

Refresh tokens are one-time-use: each refresh returns a new `refresh_token` and invalidates the previous one. Reusing an already-rotated refresh token is treated as a compromise and revokes the entire token chain.

Disabling `oauth_enabled` on the API token, or deleting the token, immediately revokes all outstanding refresh tokens. Each refresh re-validates the consenting user (still active, still holding at least the token's role for every scope it grants); otherwise the refresh is rejected and the application must obtain fresh consent.

Access tokens are stateless and remain valid until they expire (bounded by `oauth_ttl`, default 1 hour), so a revoked user loses access within one access-token lifetime.

To use the access token, pass it as a Bearer token: `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`. It carries the privileges configured on the API token, constrained to what the consenting user has.

oauth_token_request_refresh_token.description:
Rotate a refresh token for a new access token and a new refresh token. Refresh tokens are one-time-use: each refresh returns a new `refresh_token` that replaces the previous one, and the old one is invalidated. Reusing an already-rotated refresh token is treated as a compromise and revokes the entire token chain.

Each refresh re-validates the consenting user: they must still be active and must still hold at least the token's role for every scope it grants (hierarchy-aware, as at authorization time). Otherwise the refresh is rejected, the rotation chain is revoked, and the application must obtain fresh consent.

apiToken.description:
Preferred authentication method for automation and integrations. Send the API token in the HTTP `Authorization` header.

**Format**:
  `Authorization: Token {apitoken}`

**Notes**:
* An API token generated for a specific admin has the same privileges as that admin
* An API token is automatically removed if it is not used for more than 90 days
* SSO admins cannot generate admin API tokens. Use organization API tokens when scoped Org/Site privileges are needed.
apiToken.name: Authorization

csrfToken.description:
Session-based authentication for browser or login/password flows. After a successful [Login](/#operations/login) request, Mist returns a `csrftoken` cookie. Send that value in the `X-CSRFToken` header on later API requests that use the login session.

**Format**:
```
X-CSRFToken: vwvBuq9qkqaKh7lu8tNc0gkvBfEaLAmx
```

For automation, API Token authentication is preferred.
csrfToken.name: X-CSRFToken

oauth2.description:
OAuth2 authorization code flow (RFC 6749) with PKCE (RFC 7636) and rotating refresh tokens, for third-party applications (including MCP integrations) acting on behalf of a consenting user. It uses an Org API token with `oauth_enabled` set as the OAuth2 client, the `client_id` is its composite `oauth_client_id` (`<org_id>.<token_id>`). See the [Orgs OAuth2](/#operations/getOauthAuthorization) endpoints.

**Format**:
  `Authorization: Bearer {access_token}`

**Notes**:
* The access token carries the privileges configured on the API token, constrained to what the consenting user has
* The access token expires after `oauth_ttl` (default 1 hour), use the refresh token to get a new one
* No fixed scopes are defined, the scope is derived from the API token name (e.g. `custom-ServiceNow Integration`)
